question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after being diagnosed with hypertension 6 months ago. He has cut salt out of his diet and started exercising regularly, but home blood pressure measurements continue to be elevated. His blood pressure is 160/85 mm Hg. An antihypertensive medication is prescribed that decreases blood pressure by decreasing the transmembrane calcium current across vascular smooth muscle cells. Side effects include peripheral edema and flushing. Which of the following best describes why this drug does not affect skeletal muscle contraction?

options.opc: Skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor activation occurs independently of membrane depolarization
options.opd: Skeletal muscle preferentially expresses N-type and P-type calcium channels
options.ope: Skeletal muscle calcium channels do not undergo conformational change when bound to this drug

enhanced_information: The antihypertensive medication decreases transmembrane calcium current primarily through L-type calcium channels, which are abundant in vascular smooth muscle but not in skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle contraction is primarily mediated by the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via ryanodine receptors, which do not rely on extracellular calcium influx for activation. Therefore, the correct reasoning is that skeletal muscle contraction occurs independently of extracellular calcium influx, confirming that the drug does not affect skeletal muscle contraction. This aligns with the consensus that skeletal muscle lacks significant voltage-gated L-type calcium channels and relies on intracellular calcium release mechanisms.

This is in contrast to vascular smooth muscle, where L-type calcium channels play a significant role in contraction. Therefore, the most accurate statement regarding why this drug does not affect skeletal muscle contraction is that skeletal muscle contraction occurs independently of extracellular calcium influx.
